newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - China offering corn in Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - China offering corn in Indonesia.

text.p: Chinese sellers were reported to be actively offering corn below U.S. prices in Indonesia this week and local soymeal demand was strong, but other regional feed markets were quiet, traders said on Wednesday.
China is luring potential Indonesian buyers by offering corn at below U.S. origin prices but there have been no takers yet due to an expected surge in domestic output, they said.
The traders also said Indonesian feedmills had bought between 40,000 and 60,000 tonnes of soymeal in the past week, mostly from India, at just below $300 to $310 a tonne C&F.
"China has been offering corn at $148-$150 per tonne for handy-sized vessels for February to April shipments," one trader said. "That is about the U.S. price for Panamax shipments."
"But I have not heard of any deals being done yet," the trader said. "I think China will not be exporting after April when Argentina will begin shipping its crop."
The trader said Argentina was offering at $145 a tonne C&F.
He said he expected around 180,000 to 220,000 tonnes of mostly U.S. corn to arrive in Indonesia over the next two weeks. "There will be at least two Panamax shipments."
An Indonesian government official told Reuters last Friday that some 351,000 hectares planted with a high-yielding hybrid strain was expected to be harvested from January through March.

The variety had been planted in six provinces, including the key producing area of Lampung in South Sumatra. He said another 390,000 hectares would be planted between April and September, while some 900,000 hectares would be planted in 1998.
A trader said Indian origin soymeal was continuing to arrive in Indonesia, and added that demand was strong.
"The Indian soymeal was priced at $310 to $311 per tonne, which I think is on the high side," he said.
Another trader said he expected the domestic soymeal market to stay firm on strong demand from feedmills, adding that Indonesians were mostly looking to India for supply.
"About 40,000 to 60,000 tonnes of soymeal was booked last week, most of it coming from India," he said. "Some was bought at just below $300 a tonne C&F and others at $305-$310."

Data from Belawan Port in North Sumatra showed that the MV Jin Cheng Jiang was scheduled to arrive on Friday with 3,500 tonnes of soymeal from India. The MV Da Feng arrived on January 19 with 3,500 tonnes of soymeal from India. The MV Nan Jiang arrived with 5,887 tonnes of Indian soymeal on January 14.
Traders said corn and soymeal prices were stable in Jakarta at 380-390 rupiah a kg and 795-800 rupiah a kg respectively.
In Malaysia, traders said they had not heard of any purchases in the animal feeds market over the past week.
"Importers are well covered at least for February. I don't think there's an urgent need for them to buy at the moment," said a trader. "The market should stay quiet for a while."
But traders added that lower prices could attract some buying. They said importers will be in the market for one or two shipments of corn for February/March if they can buy below $150 a tonne C&F.
One trader said he expected some arrival of Chinese corn after the Lunar New Year festival in mid-February, but added that "it won't be more than 10,000 tonnes."
Bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, was slightly higher at 400-410 ringgit ($157-$161) a tonne this week, compared with 390-400 ringgit a week ago.
"A" grade wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown in the central region, was stable at 800 ringgit a tonne, while the price of low-grade wheat was also maintained at 450 ringgit a tonne.
Soymeal was virtually unchanged with local product fetching 810 ringgit a tonne amd imported soymeal 820 ringgit, both in the central region.
In Thailand, soymeal prices have edged up this week spurred by a pick-up in demand on the back of a weakening baht against the dollar, but corn prices have remained mostly steady.
A purchase of 20,000 tonnes of optional origin soymeal from South America for February shipment, was reported by traders.
The price was quoted around $309 a tonne C&F Bangkok and major Thai feed producer Betagro was said to be a buyer.
Local soymeal was quoted at around 9.40 baht a kg ($0.37) this week versus 9.20 baht a week ago, trade sources said.
"The strong dollar makes the product more expensive in baht terms. High demand also supported prices," said one trader.
Corn was quoted mostly steady at 4.25 baht a kg, barely changed from last week in modest trade.

There were market rumors of cargoes of U.S. corn bought by one major animal feed producer heading for Southeast Asia, but as the freight was concluded on an FOB basis, the exact destination was not known.
"I guess the buyer is looking for loopholes to bring the corn in. It's on FOB because if there is any problem, they can shift the product to other destinations," said another trader.
